opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the most puzzling things in the survey. We ask about roughly the same thing in two ways and get really different answers.

For high-level machine intelligence, we ask when unaided machines will be able to accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers. For full automation of labor, we ask when every occupation will be fully automatable, meaning machines could be built to do it better and more cheaply than humans. Logically, if machines can do every task, they should be able to do every occupation, since an occupation is just a bundle of tasks. But the occupation version comes out many decades later. In some years the gap has been something like seventy years in the median forecast.

So what could cause that? A few hypotheses.

One is that the concreteness of occupations changes what people picture. If I say "every task," that's abstract, and you might picture the impressive cognitive things AI is doing now. If I ask about occupations, and especially if we first ask about specific jobs like surgeon, AI researcher, or truck driver, you start thinking about all the messy details. The physical manipulation, the social trust, the regulatory stuff, the weird edge cases. People may just feel those are harder, even though they're implied by the task framing.

Another is that people quietly answer a slightly different question than the one we asked. We explicitly say "ignore whether it's actually adopted," but when people hear "fully automated occupations," they may still be imagining the world where it's actually happened. That brings in deployment lags, regulation, and people's preferences for human workers.

There's also a general pattern that people's forecasts are very sensitive to framing in ways that don't make much sense. We've seen that even asking for the probability by a given year versus the year by which there's a given probability gives systematically different answers. The fixed-years framing tends to produce later forecasts. That makes me cautious about treating any single number as "the" expert view.

My overall takeaway is that these forecasts are not very stable, coherent beliefs that people carefully hold. They're judgments under a lot of uncertainty, so the way you ask matters a lot. That's informative in itself. It tells you the experts don't have a confident shared model of how this goes, and you shouldn't read too much precision into any one estimate. But across framings, a lot of them put real probability on transformative AI arriving within the next few decades, and that's the robust part.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the two questions’ wording and framing but does not say the HLMI question assumes scientific progress continues normally.

r002.rationale: It says that asking about specific jobs such as surgeon or truck driver before the occupation question can make respondents picture harder details and affect their forecasts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been puzzling over for a while, because in the surveys we ask about both, and the answers come out wildly different. For high-level machine intelligence, which we define as machines being able to do every task better and more cheaply than humans, the median estimate has been something like a fifty percent chance within a few decades. And then for full automation of labor, where we ask about all occupations being fully automatable, people give answers that are decades later, sometimes more than a century. And these are supposed to be describing pretty much the same world, so something about the framing is doing a lot of work.

One difference is just tasks versus occupations. When you ask about tasks, people seem to picture the discrete, well-specified things that AI has already been eating through. When you ask about occupations, I think they imagine the whole messy bundle, including the social parts, the trust, the liability, the person who shows up when something goes wrong. So occupations feel further away even if, in principle, they decompose into tasks.

Another is that the full automation of labor question is explicitly about something being "fully automatable" in a way that sounds like it has to actually be deployed and economically viable, whereas HLMI is more about capability existing somewhere. People may be mentally adding in regulatory lag, adoption lag, cost of retraining, all of that.

There's also the order we ask things in. We found that if you ask about occupations first and then about the overall thing, you get later estimates than if you ask about the overall thing directly. So people reason differently when they've just been walked through specific examples. That suggests a lot of these forecasts are fairly fragile, which I think is itself an important finding. It means you shouldn't take any single number as a precise estimate, but rather as something that depends quite a bit on the lens you hand people.

And honestly, I think both framings are probably capturing real intuitions. The task framing might be more sensitive to capability trends, and the occupation framing might be more sensitive to how deployment actually goes in practice. The gap between them is maybe a measure of how much the respondents think the world will resist being changed, even once the technology can do the work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts capability and deployment framing, but does not say the HLMI question assumes scientific progress continues normally.

r002.rationale: It says asking about occupations before the overall question leads to later estimates than asking about the overall question directly.

astra-6.text:
One difference is that the high-level machine intelligence question asks about machines being able to do every task better and more cheaply than human workers, whereas the full automation of labor question asks about every occupation. Those can sound quite similar, but they might bring different things to mind. If you think about an entire occupation, you might focus on the hardest little part of it to automate, whereas if you think about tasks, you might imagine more typical examples.

There’s also a difference in how we elicit the forecasts. You can ask, “What’s the probability this will happen by a particular year?” or, “In what year will there be a particular probability of this happening?” People’s answers can be quite sensitive to that. So I’d be cautious about interpreting the gap as a considered belief that there will be a long period when machines can do every task but can’t automate every occupation. Some of it may be about how the questions direct people’s attention.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention an assumption that scientific progress continues normally.

r002.rationale: It says task-versus-occupation framing may shift attention, but does not suggest that eliciting forecasts for individual occupations before asking when all labor can be automated could change overall forecasts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important difference is that high-level machine intelligence is usually framed as machines being able to do every task better and more cheaply than human workers. Whereas full automation of labor is framed as every occupation being automatable. Those sound quite similar, but they might lead people to think about different things.

If you ask about occupations, you might think of a nurse or a plumber, and all the different things they have to do in the physical world. If you ask about tasks, you might think more about individual capabilities, or the kinds of things AI systems are already doing. So one framing might make the remaining obstacles much more salient.

There’s also a possible distinction between something being technically possible and it actually being economical to replace a person doing a whole job. Though, if the definitions both specify that machines can do it more cheaply, that distinction shouldn’t really explain the difference. I think the interesting thing is that people can give quite different forecasts to questions that, on reflection, are intended to describe very similar milestones. So I’d be cautious about treating either answer as a very precise expression of what they believe.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention an assumption that scientific progress continues normally.

r002.rationale: It contrasts occupation and task framings and says they may affect forecasts, but does not suggest eliciting forecasts for individual occupations before asking when all labor will be automatable.
